package_info.package_manager: Microsoft Office (macro-enabled Word document, distributed via ISO archive)
package_info.why_malicious: The document is weaponized with a multi-stage macro that delivers a backdoor (Havoc Demon agent) to the victim's system. It uses obfuscated VBA macros, anti-analysis techniques, and custom payload storage to evade detection, ultimately granting remote control to the attacker.

execution_context.file_location: VBA macro in Word document (EbDYTPZ.vEypm, referenced in document.xml.rels)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
For Each s In ActiveDocument.Shapes
  If s.Name = "happy" Then s.Delete
Next
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code iterates through all Shape objects in the document and deletes the one named 'happy', removing the overlay image to simulate revealing protected content.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code manipulates document content to deceive the user into believing protected information has been revealed, which is a common social engineering tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal macros should not manipulate document overlays to trick users into enabling further execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate macros may remove overlays for document formatting, but not as part of a social engineering lure.
key_indicators: Deletes overlay image upon macro enablement
Name 'happy' is arbitrary and not standard

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
If Dir("C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll") <> "" Then
  ShellExecute ...
Else
  ' Extract payload from custom XML part
End If
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code checks for the existence of a hardcoded DLL path. If present, it executes the DLL; otherwise, it proceeds to extract and decode a payload from the document's custom XML part.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Checking for and executing a DLL from a hardcoded path is a strong indicator of persistence or staged malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate macros should not execute binaries from user directories or check for malware persistence.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, enterprise macros may check for helper DLLs, but not in this context.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
For Each part In ActiveDocument.CustomXMLParts
  If part.SelectSingleNode("//TwXfx") Is Not Nothing Then
    payload = part.SelectSingleNode("//TwXfx").Text
    ' Base64 decode, add 35, xor 82
  End If
Next
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code enumerates custom XML parts in the document, locates the node 'TwXfx', extracts its content, decodes it (Base64, add 35, xor 82), and reconstructs the binary payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Storing and extracting a binary payload from custom XML parts is a stealthy technique to evade static detection and hide malicious content.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal macros do not store or reconstruct executables from document XML data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom XML parts are used for metadata, not for storing encoded binaries.
key_indicators: Custom XML node with encoded binary

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Open "C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll" For Binary As #1
Put #1, , decoded_payload
Close #1
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code writes the decoded payload to a hardcoded DLL path in the user's AppData directory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Writing an executable to a user directory is a classic malware dropper behavior.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate macros should not write arbitrary binaries to disk.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may write DLLs, but not via Office macros.
key_indicators: Uses misleading filename to masquerade as Office telemetry

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code launches the dropped payload using conhost.exe in headless mode, executing the malicious DLL.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching a dropped DLL via conhost.exe is a process injection/evasion technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Macros should not launch system processes to execute arbitrary DLLs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare in legitimate automation; not via user macros.
key_indicators: Abuse of conhost.exe for DLL execution
Headless execution to avoid user detection

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode
Read .vdata section
If RC4-encrypted, decrypt with key
If LZNT1-compressed, decompress
Parse loader config
Inject shellcode into current or new process using ZwCreateThreadEx with THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At payload execution, the loader unpacks and decrypts embedded shellcode, parses configuration, and injects the next-stage shellcode into memory using stealthy thread creation flags.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Custom in-memory unpacking, process injection, and anti-debugging flags are hallmarks of advanced malware loaders.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not inject shellcode or manipulate thread creation flags.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team tools and some security products may use similar techniques, but not in userland Office DLLs.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode
Locate PE headers in memory (0x4d 0x5a, 0x50 0x45)
Resolve LdrLoadDll, NtAllocateVirtualMemory, NtProtectVirtualMemory via API hashing
Allocate memory, load Demon agent DLL, execute in memory
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At payload execution, the shellcode locates the embedded Demon agent DLL in memory, resolves necessary APIs via hashing, allocates memory, and loads/executes the agent directly from memory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: In-memory DLL loading and API hashing are advanced evasion and anti-analysis techniques.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal code does not perform in-memory PE parsing and API resolution via hashes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team frameworks and some security tools use similar methods.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode
Generate random 256-bit key and 128-bit IV
Send HTTP/HTTPS POST to ukrtatnafta[.]org with check-in data (agent ID, command ID, AES key/IV, encrypted data)
Receive and execute C2 commands (enumerate system, execute commands, inject code, manipulate files, take screenshots, etc.)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Demon agent establishes encrypted C2 communications with a hardcoded domain, receives commands, and enables full remote control over the infected system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: C2 communication, system enumeration, and remote command execution are core backdoor behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate DLL should establish covert C2 channels or enable remote control.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team agents and penetration testing tools.

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious document and enables macros, triggering macro execution.
Macro checks for existing payload, extracts and decodes binary from custom XML if needed.
Macro launches the dropped payload (OfficeTelemetry.dll) using conhost.exe in headless mode.
Loader unpacks, decrypts, and injects shellcode into memory using anti-debugging and stealth techniques.
Shellcode (KaynLdr) locates and loads Demon agent DLL in memory.
Demon agent establishes encrypted C2 channel, receives and executes attacker commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of victim system

behavioral_signatures: Office macro extracting and decoding binary payloads from custom XML parts
Macros writing executables to user AppData directories
Macros launching DLLs via conhost.exe or similar system processes
In-memory unpacking and injection of shellcode using anti-debugging thread flags
Network connections to suspicious or hardcoded C2 domains with custom HTTP headers
AES-encrypted C2 traffic to non-standard endpoints
file_indicators: Word documents with non-standard macro storage (e.g., EbDYTPZ.vEypm instead of vbaProject.bin)
Presence of OfficeTelemetry.dll in user AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office
Custom XML parts with node names like TwXfx containing Base64-encoded data
network_indicators: Connections to ukrtatnafta[.]org and related subpaths (e.g., /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/avias.js)
HTTP/HTTPS POST requests with headers mimicking legitimate web traffic (e.g., Content-Type: application/javascript, User-Agent: Chrome/108.0.0.0)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents with macros that access custom XML parts and write executables to disk. Flag any macro that writes to AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll or launches DLLs via conhost.exe. Detect in-memory unpacking and process injection behaviors, especially those using ZwCreateThreadEx with anti-debugging flags. Monitor outbound network traffic for connections to ukrtatnafta[.]org and similar domains, especially with suspicious HTTP headers and encrypted payloads. Use YARA rules to identify custom XML nodes (e.g., TwXfx) containing Base64-encoded data in Office documents.
